items.item: On this sandbox's PostgreSQL 16, a fresh SERIALIZABLE transaction opened strictly after a sibling's commit always observed that commit, because MVCC takes its snapshot at BEGIN, not because of any documented real-time guarantee.

at.step: Reveal: measured on a real Postgres, not assumed

items.item: On the same PostgreSQL 16, a SERIALIZABLE transaction already open when a sibling committed did not observe that commit even on a later read taken after the commit finished, confirmed by the underlying table holding more rows than that transaction ever saw.

at.step: Reveal: measured on a real Postgres, not assumed

items.item: etcd's own API-guarantees documentation claims strict serializability for all KV API calls; Spanner's own paper claims external consistency, which it states is equivalent to linearizability lifted to transactions; PostgreSQL's own documentation places SERIALIZABLE one rung below both, with no real-time promise.

items.item: Two transactions with no causal link between them (neither reads what the other wrote) can be placed in either order in a serializable database's serial order, independent of which one actually ran first in real time.

items.item: A database with no concurrency at all, running every transaction to completion before the next begins, is trivially strictly serializable, because the single legal serial order and real-time order are forced to coincide.

at.step: Prove it: a database that runs every transaction literally one at a time — strictly serializable?
